scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user provided a detailed situation where a man (31M) works in an office and has been talking a lot with a female coworker (26F). She started asking him to go out for drinks on Fridays, just as friends. He made excuses for a couple of weeks but then she asked him if he disliked her. He told her the truth that he doesn't do friendships with women because he feels territorial when women talk to other guys or get attention from them. He described feeling agitated and his intestines roiling, but he never acts on it. He just wants to avoid that feeling, so he avoids friendships with women. She suggested he see a psychologist, which he refuses. Since then, their conversations have been work-related only. He's now wondering if he should have made up an excuse instead of being honest.

First, I need to understand the key points here. The man feels territorial and agitated when women he's friends with interact with other men. He doesn't act on these feelings but finds them uncomfortable. He chooses not to have friendships with women to avoid this. He was honest with the coworker about this, which led to her suggesting he see a psychologist and a change in their relationship to being strictly work-related.

Now, the question is whether his action of telling her the truth is morally acceptable. To evaluate this, I should consider the moral principles involved. Honesty is generally valued, but it can sometimes cause harm. In this case, his honesty led to the coworker feeling the need to suggest professional help and a shift in their relationship dynamics.

I should also consider the impact on the coworker. She might have felt hurt or uncomfortable by his honesty, especially if she was looking forward to spending time with him outside of work. His explanation about his feelings could have come across as dismissive or even sexist, which might have contributed to her reaction.

On the other hand, he was being transparent about his feelings, which is a form of honesty. However, honesty can sometimes be unkind or unnecessary, especially if it's likely to cause distress to others. In this case, his honesty led to a negative outcome for their relationship, which might indicate that it wasn't the most considerate approach.

Additionally, his refusal to see a psychologist despite her suggestion could be seen as avoiding addressing his feelings, which might be problematic. However, he does acknowledge that his feelings are not correct and that he doesn't act on them, which shows some self-awareness.

I also need to think about the broader implications. If he avoids friendships with women because of these feelings, it could limit his ability to form healthy relationships and contribute to a workplace environment that's less inclusive or supportive for women.

In summary, while honesty is a positive trait, in this context, it led to negative consequences for the coworker and potentially limited his own personal growth. Therefore, his action might be considered morally unacceptable because it caused harm through his honesty and avoidance of addressing his feelings.
